newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn coalition strained by split on tax cut plans.
newsitem.headline: Bonn coalition strained by split on tax cut plans.

text.p: The fragile harmony achieved by Germany's coalition government in sealing a budget deal last week was already under strain on Tuesday as differences surfaced over plans to cut a key personal tax next year.

Cutting the solidarity surcharge, or "soli", is part of a major package of government tax cuts which was thrown out of the upper house of parliament in early July by the opposition Social Democrats (SPD).
Junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) want a two-point cut in the 7.5 percent surcharge next year, even if the SPD blocks the main tax reform in parliamentary mediation.
"Reducing the solidarity surcharge would be our only tax cutting instrument," FDP parliamentary chief Hermann Otto Solms told German Radio in an interview.
The cut in the soli -- raised to finance the reconstruction of ex-communist eastern Germany -- would cost the government around seven billion marks ($3.9 billion).

Solms added the reduction in the surcharge had been agreed before the three parties in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government hammered out broader tax reform legislation. It should, if necessary, be passed separately.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel criticised the FDP for failing to promote last week's agreement on a supplementary budget for 1997 and a 1998 budget aimed at readying Germany for European economic and monetary union (EMU).
Speaking in an interview on SAT1 television to be aired later, Waigel said: "You shouldn't just raise a new issue every couple of days. The FDP isn't doing itself any favours."
Waigel said the reduction in the soli should remain part of the overall tax reform. If the tax reform fails, then "the SPD must take responsibility", he added.
A cut in the soli would, like the tax reform, require the approval of the SPD-led Bundesrat upper house of parliament.
Separately, the head of the social affairs committee of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), Rainer Eppelmann warned that CDU deputies from eastern Germany might vote against a cut in the soli.

"There is no way you can sell a cut in the solidarity surcharge in the east as a solo number," he told the Flensburger Tageblatt newspaper. -- douglas.busvine@reuters.com (Bonn 49-228-26097150) ($ = 1.784 German Marks)
